*   For each of the three edges of the base triangle, identify the corresponding vertex on the top triangle (the end of the extrusion) [S1].

The claim states that for each of the three edges of the base triangle, one must identify the corresponding vertex on the top triangle. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports this in the section 'Improved Bounding Volumes', stating: 'Ernst et al. proposed to set up touching planes for each side of the beam: three touching planes are constructed, each containing one edge of the base triangle, and one of the top vertices'. It further clarifies in the notes and text that the bounding volume is defined by selecting triangles formed by 'one triangle edge and one vertex of the opposite triangle' (where 'opposite' refers to the top triangle in the context of the extrusion). Thus, the process of identifying the corresponding top vertex for each base edge is a core part of the described method.

# Construct side triangles: each edge of base + opposite top vertex [S1]

The claim states that the method constructs side triangles by taking each edge of the base triangle and the opposite top vertex. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the section 'Improved Bounding Volumes', stating: 'as each bounding plane is defined by one triangle edge and one vertex of the opposite triangle, we can take the formed triangle directly as one side of the bounding volume.' This matches the claim exactly.

Bounding Volume Extrusion is a technique to compute tight convex hull bounding volumes for caustic beams, enabling efficient rasterization of inscattered light while minimizing fill-rate overhead [S1].

The claim states that 'Bounding Volume Extrusion' is a technique to compute tight convex hull bounding volumes for caustic beams, enabling efficient rasterization of inscattered light while minimizing fill-rate overhead. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports every part of this claim: 1) It mentions a 'tight bounding volume computation that saves fillrate when accumulating the inscattered light from caustic beams.' 2) It describes extruding beam bounding volumes in the geometry shader. 3) It details a '6-triangle convex hull method' that yields a 'tighter convex hull than the bounding prism method' and 'significantly reducing fill-rate.' 4) It confirms the purpose is to allow beams (which are bilinear patches) to be rasterized efficiently.
